prompt: What does joining the points of a line chart tell the reader?

choices.text: That the values are categories
choices.why: Joining categories draws slopes that mean nothing.

choices.text: That the axis starts at zero
choices.why: Joining says nothing about the axis.

choices.text: That they are one thing measured again and again, in order
choices.why: Right. And the slope between two points is how fast it changed.

choices.text: That the values were measured exactly
choices.why: Precision is a separate matter.

prompt: Somebody draws a line through the five regions, Southeast to North. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: The slopes between regions mean nothing
choices.why: Right. Regions are categories, and categories want bars.

choices.text: Lines need at least twelve points
choices.why: A line can have three points if they are moments in time.

choices.text: The line should have markers on each point
choices.why: Markers would not fix a slope between categories.

choices.text: The regions are not sorted by size
choices.why: Sorted or not, the slopes between them invent a rate that does not exist.

prompt: March is missing from a monthly series. What should the line do there?

choices.text: Join February to April in a straight line
choices.why: That draws a March that never existed.

choices.text: Drop to zero for March
choices.why: Zero is a measurement; missing is not.

choices.text: Break, or mark the month as missing
choices.why: Right. A straight line across the gap invents values nobody measured.

choices.text: Repeat February's value
choices.why: Repeating a value also invents one.

prompt: Why may a line chart's vertical axis start above zero when a bar chart's may not?

choices.text: Line charts are only used for small numbers
choices.why: Lines are used for numbers of every size.

choices.text: Readers ignore the axis of a line chart
choices.why: They read positions against it, which is why it must be labelled.

choices.text: There is no difference; both must start at zero
choices.why: The rule belongs to marks whose length carries the number.

choices.text: A line shows position, not length
choices.why: Right. Nothing in it is read as a length from zero.

prompt: The same line looks steady in a wide, short frame and explosive in a narrow, tall one. What did Cleveland propose?

choices.text: Always draw line charts square
choices.why: A square frame is no guarantee; the data decides the ratio.

choices.text: Choose the frame so the important slopes sit near 45 degrees
choices.why: Right. Banking to 45 degrees, because slopes are compared most accurately there.

choices.text: Make every chart as wide as the page
choices.why: Width alone can flatten a line until nothing is visible.

choices.text: Start every axis at zero
choices.why: That is about the range, not the shape of the frame.

prompt: Two line charts of two regions' sales sit side by side in a report, each with its own axis range fitted to its data. What is the risk?

choices.text: None, as long as each axis is labelled
choices.why: The labels are right, and readers still compare the pictures, not the labels.

choices.text: Readers compare the slopes, which the two ranges made incomparable
choices.why: Right. Charts meant to be compared must share range and aspect ratio.

choices.text: The lines will be too thin to read
choices.why: Thickness is not affected by the axis range.

choices.text: Fitted ranges are forbidden on line charts
choices.why: A fitted range is fine on one chart. The problem is comparing two.

prompt: One region's line is the story and four others are context. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Five strong colours and a legend
choices.why: That makes every line compete equally.

choices.text: Remove the four other lines
choices.why: They are the context that makes the one line unusual.

choices.text: Make all five lines thicker
choices.why: Thicker lines tangle more, not less.

choices.text: Colour the one, grey the rest
choices.why: Right. The reader knows where to look before asking.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer a name at the end of each line to a legend?

choices.text: The name sits where the eye already is
choices.why: Right. A legend sends the eye away and back, once per line.

choices.text: Legends are forbidden in line charts
choices.why: They are allowed; they are just slower to use.

choices.text: End labels make the lines straighter
choices.why: They change nothing about the lines.

choices.text: Software cannot draw legends for more than three series
choices.why: Software draws legends of any length.

prompt: In a dual-axis chart, who decides where the two lines cross?

choices.text: The data, since crossings are measurements
choices.why: Two series in two scales never meet in the data.

choices.text: The reader, by where they look
choices.why: The crossing is drawn on the page whatever the reader does.

choices.text: Nobody; crossings are random
choices.why: They are fully determined by the two ranges chosen.

choices.text: Whoever chose the two axis ranges
choices.why: Right. A different pair of ranges moves the crossing or removes it.

prompt: matplotlib's twinx fitted the left axis to 5,016 to 8,354 and the right to 395 to 1,495. What does the reader see?

choices.text: North as a thin line near the floor
choices.why: That happens only when both axes share a range.

choices.text: Southeast twice as tall as North
choices.why: Each line fills its own axis, so neither is taller.

choices.text: Two lines of the same height
choices.why: Right. A far smaller region is drawn as tall as the largest.

choices.text: An error, because the ranges overlap
choices.why: matplotlib draws it without complaint.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson offer instead of a dual axis? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Index both series to 100 at a common start
choices.why: Right. One axis, compared honestly.

choices.text: A third axis for a third series
choices.why: That multiplies the problem.

choices.text: A scatterplot of one series against the other
choices.why: Right, when the question is whether they move together.

choices.text: Two panels stacked, sharing the time axis
choices.why: Right. Each keeps its own scale without inviting a crossing.

prompt: Orders and average delivery minutes are drawn on two axes, and the lines cross in June. What does the crossing mean?

choices.text: That orders equalled minutes in June
choices.why: Different units cannot be equal.

choices.text: Nothing: the units differ
choices.why: Right. Orders and minutes cannot be equal; the crossing comes from the ranges.

choices.text: That deliveries slowed because orders rose
choices.why: A crossing on two scales is not evidence of a cause.

choices.text: That June is the busiest month
choices.why: The crossing says nothing about either series' peak.

prompt: A region had 445 orders in January 2024 and 1,445 in December 2025. What is its index in December 2025, with January 2024 as 100? Answer to one decimal place.
On the indexed chart North ends at 325 and Southeast at 159. What can the reader conclude?

choices.text: North now sells more than Southeast
choices.why: Southeast still sells more than five times as much.

choices.text: North sells about twice as much as Southeast
choices.why: The indices compare each region with its own start, not with each other.

choices.text: North grew faster
choices.why: Right. Indexing compares growth; it says nothing about size.

choices.text: Southeast is shrinking
choices.why: 159 is above 100: it grew by 59%.

prompt: Why is December a poor base month for indexing Horta's orders?

choices.text: It is the last month of the year
choices.why: Position in the year is not the problem; being unusual is.

choices.text: It is a peak, so every later month looks like a fall
choices.why: Right. Pick an ordinary month and name it.

choices.text: Indices must start in January
choices.why: Any month can be the base; it should be an ordinary one.

choices.text: December has too few orders
choices.why: December has the most orders, which is exactly the problem.

prompt: A product went from 2 orders to 10. What index does that give, with the first value as 100?
hint: A small base makes a large index from a small change.

prompt: Find each of these in the dual-axis chart.

labels.text: the axis the solid line is read against
the axis the dashed line is read against
a crossing that the two axis ranges decided
the first year's December peak of the solid line

hint: Each axis is drawn in the colour of its line.

prompt: Match each situation to what the lesson recommends.

pairs.left: two series of very different sizes, compared for growth
one series is the story among five
pairs.right: highlight it and grey the rest
five small charts on the same axes

pairs.left: a series with sharp seasonal spikes

prompt: Cleveland's rule of choosing a chart's proportions so the important slopes sit near 45 degrees is called ___ to 45 degrees.
A manager shows a chart where marketing spend and revenue, on two axes, rise together and cross in March, as proof the campaign worked. What is the strongest objection?

choices.text: Revenue should be on the left axis
choices.why: Swapping sides changes nothing about the problem.

choices.text: The ranges were chosen; a scatterplot would test it
choices.why: Right. The likeness of two lines on two axes is drawn, not measured.

choices.text: The chart needs a legend
choices.why: A legend would name the lines and leave the ranges as they are.

choices.text: March is too early to judge a campaign
choices.why: Perhaps, but the chart's design is the deeper problem.

prompt: Horta's total orders went from 10,552 in January 2024 to 20,586 in December 2025. What is December 2025's index, with January 2024 as 100? Answer to the nearest whole number.
